slides.title: The shop till
slides.text: At the till, a dollar is a whole of 100 cents, and coins are its parts. A quarter is 25 cents, a dime is 10 cents, a nickel is 5 cents and a penny is 1 cent. Four quarters fill the dollar exactly.

slides.title: One dollar, four quarters
slides.text: A quarter is worth 25 cents, and a dollar is worth 100 cents. Watch the bar fill: each quarter paints 25 of the 100 cents. Coins are just measures with pictures on them.

visual.label: A bar for one dollar split into four equal parts of 25 cents, one for each quarter

focus.cue: Two quarters: half the dollar, 50 cents.
Four quarters fill the dollar: 100 cents.

slides.title: Worked example: change for a toy
slides.text: Rough first: the toy costs more than half a dollar, so the change is less than 50 cents. You pay 100 cents for a 65-cent toy. The change is the gap between 65 and 100 on the bar.
steps: Count up from 65 to 70: that is 5 cents
Count up from 70 to 100: that is 30 cents

visual.label: A bar model for change: a dollar bar on top, and below it a bar where 65 cents is the price and the dashed part is the change

focus.cue: You hand over one whole dollar: 100 cents.
The price takes 65 of the 100 cents.
The empty part is the change. Count up from 65 to find it.

slides.title: The Jumble at the till
slides.text: The Jumble tried to help by ringing up a sticker priced at $2.05. It charged 235 cents, as if the price said $2.35. The zero matters: it holds the tens place, so $2.05 is 205 cents, not 235.

slides.title: Stretch: fewest coins
slides.text: Stretch: make 87 cents using the fewest coins you can. Quarters first, then dimes, then nickels, then pennies. How few did you manage? Stretch work is never in the check.

slides.title: Your mission
slides.text: Open Brain Board at Practice Board and score 3,000 points to finish. It opens straight on your Money board, and your board saves as you go. Get there your way: lots of easy tiles, or fewer hard ones. Count every change answer up from the price before you pick a tile.
